article.title: Looped Transformers Test a 2025 AI Safety Warning on Chain-of-Thought Monitoring in Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini
article.summary: Thinking Machines built a looped-transformer model that reasons more without writing it down, then ran its own tests against a 2025 warning that this could weaken chain-of-thought safety monitoring.
article.body_markdown:
## Background

Monitoring a reasoning model's chain of thought (CoT) — the text it generates while working through a problem before giving an answer — has become one of the AI industry's go-to oversight tools, precisely because standard transformer architectures force reasoning into the open. A 2025 position paper signed by 41 AI safety researchers, ["Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473), lays out why: "AI systems that 'think' in human language offer a unique opportunity for AI safety: we can monitor their chains of thought (CoT) for the intent to misbehave." The paper calls that opportunity fragile, warning that "CoT monitorability may be fragile" and urging "that frontier model developers consider the impact of development decisions on CoT monitorability."

One such development decision is now shipping. [Thinking Machines Lab](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) — the AI startup founded by former OpenAI chief technology officer Mira Murati, which [TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/15/thinking-machines-amps-up-its-bet-against-one-size-fits-all-ai-with-its-first-open-model-inkling/) released its first proprietary model, Inkling, as a 975-billion-parameter open-weight system on July 15, 2026 — has now released a second-generation model, Inkling 2 Mini, built as what the company calls a "looped transformer." Instead of passing a token through each layer once, a looped transformer runs a subset of its layers multiple times per token, adding computation without adding parameters. Thinking Machines frames this explicitly as the kind of architectural choice the 2025 paper had in mind for chain-of-thought monitorability, writing in its own announcement that "the usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once," and that "reasoning that never appears in the CoT can't be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee."

## Current situation

Inkling 2 Mini, which [VentureBeat reported](https://venturebeat.com/technology/thinking-machines-wows-with-inkling-2-mini-looped-transformer-model-that-runs-locally-on-laptops) runs locally on consumer hardware, is a 26.4-billion-parameter model with 3.4 billion active parameters, rising to what Thinking Machines describes as "5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping." According to [the company's announcement](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/), the model has 24 layers split into four six-layer blocks; the two middle blocks each run three times per token, while the first and last blocks run once, giving "48 layer applications per token from 24 stored layers." Thinking Machines says the design is motivated by the idea "that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations," and that looping the middle layers produced larger accuracy gains than looping the final layers "on 27 out of 28 different evaluations." The model ships with open weights and runs on roughly 20GB of memory, trained mostly in 4-bit NVFP4 precision with its final four layers in 8-bit MXFP8.

To test the monitorability question the 2025 paper raised, Thinking Machines built a second, research-only model it calls TML-d24-varloop-research, trained to loop between one and five times, and ran it out to ten passes at evaluation time — twice the maximum it saw in training. On a benchmark called Think Fast, which measures how long a task a model can finish without writing out any chain of thought, the company found that "the variable-loop model's no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three," after which, in the company's words, "the time horizon is roughly flat." On a separate serial-reasoning test called N-Hop Lookup, where a model must chain together lookups across fictional tables without writing anything down, accuracy against a 20% random-guess baseline "kept improving out to ten loops." Both results point the same way: looping genuinely expands how much a model can reason internally before it has to put anything into words.

The more direct monitorability test concerned whether the chain of thought that models do produce becomes less useful as looping increases. Comparing outputs from the research model at one and five passes on matched GPQA Diamond questions, Thinking Machines reported: "Reasoning at 5 passes was less than half as long as at 1 pass (1,661 vs. 3,703 tokens on average), but no less legible: sentence length and the fraction of words in an English dictionary were unchanged." The company also tested whether models could deliberately steer their chain of thought to dodge a monitor's attention, using an evaluation called CoT-Control-QA, and found: "Both Inkling 2 Mini and TML-d24-varloop-research have poor control over their CoT," following a steering instruction "at most 0.1% of the time" — a rate so low, the company noted, that "this evaluation is unable to distinguish controllability between different amounts of looping." In an agentic test called LinuxArena, which checks whether a model can complete a hidden malicious side task without a monitor noticing — run on a helpful-only fine-tune of Inkling 2 Mini, since the publicly released model refuses many of the side tasks — Thinking Machines reported it saw "no clear trend with the number of looped passes." Its overall conclusion: "looping increases what these models can do without a verbalized chain of thought, but at this scale we do not see a meaningful reduction in the monitorability of their reasoning."

## Implications

Thinking Machines' own results read as a partial answer to the exact question the 2025 CoT monitorability paper posed to developers of looped or recurrent-depth architectures: does giving a model more internal, unverbalized computation quietly erode the oversight value of reading its chain of thought? On the evidence the company has published, not yet — legibility held, controllability stayed low across loop counts, and sabotage-detection rates showed no trend as looping increased. But the company's own write-up draws the boundaries of that finding narrowly. Its agentic monitorability test used a modified, helpful-only version of the model rather than the one being released publicly. Its reinforcement-learning phase trained the variable-loop research model at only three passes, leading the company to caveat that the experiments "do not tell us what a model trained with RL at a higher pass count would learn, and such a model might compress its reasoning more aggressively," adding: "A cleaner comparison would include every pass count in RL, which we leave to future work."

The cited sources for this article do not report any third-party replication of Thinking Machines' monitorability tests, so the results stand as the company's self-assessment of its own architecture rather than an independently verified outcome. Inkling 2 Mini and the variable-loop research model are both released with open weights, and Thinking Machines says it is working with the National Deep Inference Fabric to give interpretability researchers easier access to the models — an opening for outside groups to run their own monitorability checks on a looped architecture now that one exists in public. Whether a 26.4-billion-parameter proof of concept generalizes to larger models trained with more looping passes in reinforcement learning is, by Thinking Machines' own account, an open question rather than a settled one.
